beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/Mongo connection string from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never commit secrets into code or logs; provide a .env.example with a placeholder only.

Create a single shared MongoClient/MotorClient at application startup and reuse it for all requests (do not create a new client per request); configure pool size to match FastAPI concurrency (maxPoolSize).

Pin and verify compatible driver/ODM versions (Motor, PyMongo, Beanie) that match the cluster wire protocol (MongoDB server version) to avoid import/runtime incompatibilities; add the exact versions to requirements.txt.
Use TLS/SSL for connections and avoid turning certificate validation off; prefer the connection string supplied by the service which includes tls options.

Enforce retention with a TTL index on a date field (e.g., expireAt or createdAt) and remember MongoDB TTL deletions are background/approximate (granularity and delay), so do not rely on sub-minute precision.

Model consent as append-only history inside the document for audit (push new entries to a history array and keep a derived current state fields like currentPreferences and consentVersion) but guard against unbounded array growth—if history may be large, store it in a separate collection.

Add indexes to support the most frequent queries: e.g., unique/composite index on (customerId, channel) or (customerId, current) and a single-field index on customerId to get the current preference quickly; include consentVersion or lastUpdated if you query by it.

Prevent document size explosion: consider capping history array length, compressing history entries, or moving history to a child collection when appending would risk hitting the BSON 16MB document limit.

Use atomic single-document updates (e.g., findOneAndUpdate with $push and $set) to append history and update derived current state in one operation, avoiding race conditions and minimizing the need for multi-document transactions.

Implement optimistic concurrency control for updates that must not be lost (e.g., include a consentVersion or a lastUpdated timestamp in the filter of findOneAndUpdate) to avoid lost updates under concurrent requests.

Enable driver-level retry options (retryWrites=true, retryReads=true) and implement application-level retries with exponential backoff for transient network/timeout errors; be mindful of idempotency when retrying writes.
Prefer reading from the primary for the freshest consent state; set readPreference=primary (or design for eventual consistency if you can tolerate stale reads).

If you need multi-document atomicity (e.g., update user profile plus consent across collections), use transactions but restrict their scope and payload size; verify MongoDB API/cluster version supports multi-document transactions in Azure DocumentDB.
When using an ODM like Beanie, rely on its Pydantic models for input validation but also enforce server-side validation or schema validators at the collection level for defense in depth.
Mask or redact connection strings and secrets in logs, exceptions, and telemetry; use structured logging with sensitive field scrubbing.

Create and maintain appropriate indexes for queries used by API endpoints (e.g., queries to fetch current preferences by customerId should be covered by an index) and periodically inspect query plans (explain) to detect COLLSCANs.

For vector search, store embedding vectors in a dedicated field with fixed dimensionality and create the provider-specific vector index (specifying dimension, metric, and engine parameters like HNSW/IVF) before querying; keep vectors normalized per the index requirements.

Avoid mixing synchronous pymongo and asynchronous Motor clients in the same process for runtime usage; if you must use both (e.g., for seeding), keep them separated and prefer one for the app runtime to avoid compatibility and event-loop issues.

Provision appropriate throughput (RU/s or instance sizing) for expected write-heavy workloads (e.g., consent updates) and consider autoscale or appropriate tier to avoid throttling; monitor for 429/Throttling errors and back off.
Log and audit consent changes (actor id, timestamp, ip, reason) in each appended history entry to provide a clear, queryable audit trail; treat audit entries as immutable records.
